title: The Jimmy Forrest "Night Train" story again, with Lloyd Glenn and Imperial
summary: Callender gives the label details for his A&R work and retells passing on Forrest.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Also you said that you were trying to think of the label that you recorded with Lloyd Glenn on.

Imperial. The Imperial label. I was the A&R man. I think this was the early Fifties. Yeah, this was in the early Fifties before I started working for (Down Beat, not IMPERIAL). Dolphin. Jack Lauderdale owned the label, and Lloyd Glenn was his featured artist, and Lloyd Glenn sold a lot of records for them. As a matter of fact, he made them a lot of money.

Anyway, I was going to tell a story about he and I taking a trip to St. Louis to see Jimmy Forrest, on Clark Terry's recommendation. So we get to St. Louis, and we go hear Jimmy Forrest, and I wanted to buy him right away. Because he was playing "Happy Go Lucky Local" which later became "Night Train". Remember that?
Yeah. I think we talked about that on another reel.

Anyhow, he didn't buy it, and later we went on to Chicago and did some other things with...this name escapes me, too. Anyway, we went to Chicago, and recorded Clark Terry and some other people... I can't remember the guy's name at the moment, so I'll have to insert that somewhere.

In Imperial, yes. And two months later Universal (I think that was the name of the label) came out with "Night Train," and the rest of that is history. Every time I see him I say, "See, you should listen to somebody that knows." He missed a windfall by passing that one up.
